They were ostensibly Yugoslav, but I saw privately own trucks with Ruma licence plates, and they were soldiers and reservists. They were all mixed up and they passed through on their way to Zvornik. And when I was taken away to be detained in Celopek, in front of the Celopek cultural club there were hedgehogs. There was a hedgehog barricade. And there were about eight tanks and a self-propelled vehicle and an APC parked in that courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now I'm going to give you so some precise data and you'll confirm whether it's correct or not, but let me draw your attention before that to something else. I assume you did your regular military service, and even if you didn't, you must know that in case of an imminent threat of war or a state of war the JNA has the right to temporarily requisition equipment from companies, enterprises, and so on, and they were able to requisition a certain number of trucks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to my information as early as the 28th of February, 1992, a tank battalion, which was part of a whole tank brigade which moved to the area of the Zvornik Corps from the north of Croatia or from Slovenia, maybe from Crtnica [phoen], but I'm not sure, and one battalion of this tank brigade was deployed in Zvornik. One tank company around the bridge of Karakaj, one company in the village of Celopek, and one company in the village of Pilica. What do you think about this? Do you think that this piece of information is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, these companies which you say that arrived from Croatia, that is correct. And that they were deployed in the courtyard of the Celopek cultural centre, I don't deny that because -- well, I didn't see what soldiers were there, whether they were young or not. But in that march, which may have been before or later, those who went from the direction of Bijeljina towards Zvornik there were tanks there where I know there were young soldiers. But let me tell you, at that time whether there were conscripts of 30 or 40 years of age serving in the JNA. I'm asking you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to have a break because we've been sitting for an hour and a half. We'll now have a 20-minute break, and we'll resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We finished off before the break with a question you asked me, where these elderly people of 30, 35, 40, how come they were in the JNA. That's what you asked me. And let me give you an answer. I'm going to answer you by posing another question, and it's this: Do you know that throughout 1991 and the beginning of 1992, from time to time the JNA conducted a mobilisation of its reserve force on the territory of almost the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There were no barracks where I lived, where I was, so I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know about these mobilisation call-ups from time to time? And the fact is that most of the Serbs responded to the call-up, whereas the Muslims tried to avoid it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Nobody called us up. Whether anybody called the Serbs in our parts, I don't know. All I did was ask you a question. When the column was passing by there were people who were between the ages of 30 and 40, maybe even older in this mixed column. Now, when they were mobilised and who mobilised and all the rest of it, I don't know. Perhaps there was a law that governed this in the JNA but I didn't know about it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you do your military service yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: After that did you ever go for any additional military training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Fine. If you don't any military training, you probably don't know how the JNA functioned and this call-up of reservists, but if the JNA really did call up its reservists, isn't it quite logical that in the same JNA column you would have young soldiers who were doing their regular military service and the reservists who had been called up and were slightly older? That's quite logical.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I said that I saw these people ranging between these ages. Now, what is logical is up to the Court, what they're going to accept and that's all I can say. I saw the people. Those were the people. Now, whether they should have been there or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Can we have a look at the document we were looking at a moment ago. Is it still on our screens? I don't seem to have it up on e-court. Tell me what button to press, please. It doesn't seem to be here. Ah, I can see it now. Yes. Thank you. Now, let's look at the third paragraph of that statement of yours, and I will read it out slowly and then we're going to discuss certain issues that are of interest there. "Up until the 7th of May, I was at my home," and then you mention what village, "when a Chetniks patrol came in front of our house,

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Tell me who you recognised in what you call a Chetnik patrol.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first have to state this: It says Chetnik patrol there. Now, if I signed it, I don't usually use -- well, I never mentioned this name "Chetniks" throughout my life, but it seems to say that there. It's been written down there. Now, whether he was directly a Chetnik or not, anyway, he was a Serb from my village, and his name was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't have to give us his name. Now, how many members did the patrol number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were they all Serbs from your own place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: One was from your village, the rest went; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, an additional question. Was it usual on the Muslim side for almost all the soldiers in regular conversations to refer to Chetniks and Chetnik forces and the JNA as a Serbo-Chetnik army and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I said that I lived in that place where there was a mixed population and we got on well as I said, but there was a certain distance in relationships afterwards. I don't know who behaved like that. Maybe in places where there was just a single ethnicity, Serb areas or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't think you have to justify yourself for saying Chetnik patrol. That's nothing rude or insulting. It's rude if somebody is -- it's bad if somebody is a criminal, but it's a nice Serbian tradition which Serbs are proud of, although some people tend and want to denigrate it. But you don't have to justify yourself for using that expression.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not justifying myself. You said yourself, and I said at the beginning, that not all people are the same. Not all people are Chetniks, and that not all people committed evil deeds. But my heart does hurt when I think of those who perpetrated crimes, especially crimes against myself and my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's move on through the text. You say that "they loaded us up onto a van and drove us to Celopek where they put us up; i.e., detained us, on the premises of the Ekonomija or the Agricultural Cooperative Celopek. Upon entering the room I immediately noticed traces of blood which led me to conclude that there were some citizens who were detained in that same room before us and that they had been physically abused there. The next day we were moved from this room to another room, which was a little bigger with a concrete floor, and there were 19 more civilians inside it. So that if you add us three, that made a total of 22 people in that one room. Immediately after that, the Chetniks came into this room. I don't know their names or surnames, but they were all from Serbia. Most of them from Kraljevo, Valjevo, and Loznica, and they wore camouflage uniforms with insignia of the White Eagles. This insignia was round, in the shape of a badge with the two-headed eagle, and they had white bandannas over their heads. These Chetniks demanded that while they were filming all this with a camera and with" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Seselj, you made a mistake in reading here. The white bandannas or bandages or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I didn't make a mistake. I thought it was a printing error. The typist that typed this out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But you should read what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It said: "They had white bandannas, povezi," and then there's a typing mistake there, over their heads." So all I did was to skip over these superfluous words which are quite obviously a typo. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So they had these white bandannas over their heads or scarves over their heads. That's the substance of it. Somebody else wrote this, not you. I assume that a typist typed it out. Now it goes on to say the following: "These Chetniks demanded from us that while they filmed us with cameras and to say how we were members of Alija's Warriors and that we fought at Kula Grad and that we had been captured as combatants, although we were arrested in our homes as civilians without weapons. And that's what we wanted to stress. We wanted to stress the truth. But these Chetniks forbade us to say that." Is that what you said in your statement? Is there anything that's superfluous there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's it. That's what it was. And if I say that, then that's how it was. I don't remember exactly or the exact words, but that's how it was. It says there that all of them, everyone. They didn't all wear these white scarves over their heads because they would be Arabs and, I apologise for saying that, they would be Arabs if they looked like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, they're not wearing bandages. They're wearing these white scarves as a component part of the Arabic national costume. It can be white, black and white, or red and white.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, all right, but that's what I said, because as some people -- individuals wore that on their heads, not everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Can we go on to page 2, because you're not questioning anything there. So let's start at the beginning there. "In Celopek," that is to say -- and I can't read what it says there. Can you help me out here? There's a word here that's not quite clear. "In Celopek or the agriculture farm," is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: "Together with the others I was detained from the 7th of May to the 12th of May, 1992. I was detained. During all that time, I was physically abused, and I also personally saw," and then you say who the two other people are who were also -- who were also abused. And now I come to the most important part of your statement: "Namely, one day you go on to say, that is, on the 12th of May in the morning, the Chetnik whom they called Vojvoda and his surname was Repic, and I don't know his first name, together with another Chetnik called Zoks took out," and then they say who they took out and beat. So as far as this Vojvoda is concerned, and this Vojvoda is mentioned in your other statements as well, in this freshest of statements you say that his surname was Repic. Isn't that right? So you couldn't have thought that name up, conjured it up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that was -- well, there were stories going round what he looked like, so that Repic might be a mistake, meaning Repic -- Repic like a little pony-tail. I've never actually heard anybody call somebody Repic. So it was a Vojvoda with this pony-tail, rep, rep being pony-tail, with this man Zoks. So maybe I said the diminutive of "rep" which is "repic" meaning a small pony-tail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You signed statement and you state that his surname was Repic, and there's no typo there. It says: "His surname is Repic." And I claim that this is not just by chance because you knew for certain that they called him Repic. Isn't that right, Mr. VS-1015?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's not quite right, because at that time and in all that chaos when I gave the statement can you imagine the state I was in and all the rest of it? So a mistake could happen, could occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, bearing in mind your state and everything you experienced and lived through, quite possibly you forgot something but that you fabricated the name of this Chetnik Vojvoda, his surname being Repic. I don't believe that. You couldn't have thought that up. You said it the way you remembered it. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, all right. Maybe that's how it was too. Maybe somebody talked to us and then the name Repic came up. So that's how I came to say it. But once again, I would like to say specifically I can't say I knew it was Repic, that his actual name was Repic 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't know this 100 per cent because Repic is not his surname but his nickname was indeed Repic. So you heard some other people refer to him and call him by this nickname Repic. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: His surname is not Repic. His name is Dusan Vuckovic, and his nickname was Repic or Pony-tail, and he belonged to the Yellow Wasp formation. Have you heard about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not then. I heard about them later on, quite a long time after the war, because I didn't stay in Bosnia. I went off.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did you hear that already in 1993 in Serbia a group of people were taken to trial for crimes committed against Muslim prisoners and civilians in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear that one of them was called Dusan Vuckovic and that his nickname was Repic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear that at the time he was convicted to a prison term and that he spent time in prison doing his sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear that he was arrested again for other crimes for which -- which were not known in Serbia in 1993, so he was supposed to be tried again with another group that was being tried in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that -- or, rather, I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did you hear that about two years ago this same man, Dusan Vuckovic nicknamed Repic, committed suicide in prison? I think he hanged himself, anyway he committed suicide.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard he committed suicide, and you've just told me that he hanged himself. So, well, if he did what he did, then that's sort of God's retribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I agree -- I agree that there is God's retribution and punishment for any crimes that you do in life. Anyway, we've identified this man and you've heard of him even at the time that you were tortured in Zvornik when you were beaten up and when you had a bad time of it, and you heard after the war that this man was tried and that he committed suicide in prison. Now you've confirmed that you heard all about that, and then somebody suggested to you that in your later statements, and in talking to The Hague OTP, that you shouldn't mention this surname or nickname Repic at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down again, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I do not believe it was the witness's evidence that he heard the name Repic while he was being tortured. I don't know if it's a translation problem. The witness, I believe, stated that he had not heard the name Repic used at the time he was in the camp, but he only learned it later. He did not hear it while he were in the camp. So the question -- the premise on the question is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness challenged that and denied it, and then he confirmed that he heard people call this man Repic, and I assume that it was properly recorded in the transcript. There's no reason. Well, anyway, everything has been videotaped and so on, so you can check it out and I don't suppose you'll delete this from the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-1015, do you know what AID is, AID?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: AID, AID, it's an abbreviation for an organisation of Muslim authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. This is the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The official title is The Agency for Information and Documentation, AID. Have you ever heard of the existence of that agency under Muslim controlled territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was in detention. I was incarcerated, and for a long time, almost 15 months, and I ended up in Batkovici, and then I was transferred for a few months to the federation and from there I went to another place, so I have been excluded from all those events in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How long did you live in the federation before you went abroad, to live abroad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was from the 21st of July, 1993, when I was exchanged, until the 1st of May, 1994, when I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did any other representatives of the Muslim authorities call you in for interviews, the police, state officials, the same thing, apart from the state commission that you couldn't remember the name of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember but I don't believe so because I was there for a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you couldn't even remember the representative of the state commission for collecting facts about war crimes you forgot that too, and that was an important moment in your life because it was the first time that you told your entire story to everyone, what happened to you and what happened to the other Muslims who were together with you while you were incarcerated in the area of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That is the document, but you didn't give any statement before this statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what are you challenging? You have the document there. There's everything that I said. Now, if I forgot something after so many years -- now, Mr. Seselj, can you tell me what you did -- you had for breakfast seven days ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What did you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I had muesli with calcium milk and artificial sugar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in those units you know what you have for breakfast.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, what units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, where you've been put up, where you're accommodated, that unit there. I apologise but that's common knowledge I assume. And all I wanted to say, Mr. Seselj, that it's been 17 years. If somebody were to say -- give you a date or something like that, well, you forget. Can you imagine what a long time that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-1015, what we -- the food we're given in Scheveningen is probably not much better than the food you were given when you were incarcerated. Perhaps it's just worse, and we're forced to make our own -- prepare our own food.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry for everything you lived through and experienced and I said that I consider that everything you told the Muslim authorities is the truth because it was to the best of your recollections when your recollections were fresh. The problem is that other people added on to your recollections later on with things that you did not see and experience and then through their suggestive methods they made you -- made you say those things, because your memory must have been fresher five or six months later, whereas now we have much more detailed recollections suddenly 15 years on which do not correspond to the truth. And somebody suggested to you to keep quiet about this surname or nickname Repic. That's what I wanted to point out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I say with full responsibility that that's not what I wanted I didn't want to keep quiet about that. Now how that happened, how that came too pass, I really can't say. I can't remember all the details and that was not my wish. And I say that full responsibility before this Trial Chamber that I didn't do so intentionally that nobody prevailed upon me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. I don't want to continue arguing. I have every respect for the suffering you went through whether you believe me or not, and that is why I don't want to treat you as I would treat perhaps some other witness on the Serb side for whom I had ascertained that he was given false testimony. So I have every sympathy for the troubles you went through, but do you now confirm that somebody really did refer to this man and call him Repic? Have I refreshed your memory now, managed to jog it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I say I don't know. I don't know what happened at the time. Anyway this man Repic appeared through the stories and what people said and that was how it was expressed in that case. Now, they did address him as Vojvoda, this person Repic. Zoks referred to him and called him Vojvoda. He said Vojvoda, sir. Then he went and to open the door to him, and the soldiers standing next to him, he said, "The Vojvoda wants to tell you that if you go and work, you'll stay alive. He said you have to go to work. You have to go and work." And he said, "You can't eat bread free unless you do some work." And the word used was leb, l-e-b. That's the dialect that was used. I know that is used in Serbia because in Bosnia-Herzegovina we don't use that same word. We say hljeb meaning bread or kruh meaning bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I belive what you're saying. I'm not questioning that. But I don't think you understand why your identification of the man is important, the man called Repic. It is important to me because The Hague OTP, along with other witnesses, wishes to move this identity to some other person. Now, I agree that this man introduced himself as Vojvoda, and the gang around him did address him as Vojvoda, but he wasn't any Vojvoda, any role Vojvoda. Do you believe me when I tell you that? He just liked to call himself Vojvoda, self proclaimed, and he had a name and he had this nickname of Repic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You've just reminded me of is something. He wasn't important as far as you're concerned. I believe you when you say that. But he was important as far as we were concerned and here's why: When before that -- when the soldier entered on that 12th into the room and said "Kneel down with your forehead to the floor, on the concrete floor, with your hands behind your backs and you're to wait until Vojvoda makes the -- the Vojvoda makes decision." And when he entered he said, "And what are you doing? Why are you bowing down? This is not a mosque." That means that at that point Vojvoda, the so-called Vojvoda as you said, was even greater than the Vojvoda you would call a Vojvoda whereas you're denying that he was a real Vojvoda but a false Vojvoda. But it didn't matter to us whether he was true or false. If he did what he did, that's the name we remembered him by.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So we're not disputing anything you and I. I completely agree with what you say and the crimes that you've described resemble the kind of things that this person really did do, and his brother testified about that as well, and his brother distanced himself from him during the legal proceedings. So I'm not questioning the veracity of your story at all. All I'm interested is establishing this identification, identity, because some other witnesses here along with support from the Prosecution are trying to change his identity to accuse somebody else falsely of being Repic. So that's why I'm insisting on this point. That's why it's important for me, and that's why we can move on and see what happened to you next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well if we move on then that's fine, but I do take issue with the allegation that the Prosecution is trying to influence --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving interpretation. No interpretation at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor was objecting and saying that the Prosecution was not in any way trying to influence the witness. This is what Mr. Marcussen has told us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So we've arrived at this fact then that Repic and this Chetnik named Zoks took you out and two other men, people, two other Muslims. That's how I'm going to refer to them, because they were Muslims, not to have to mention their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It does not reflect the witness evidence. The witness said a person named -- referred to as Vojvoda was taken out -- took them out together with another person. The witness has not confirmed that the name of the person who he refers to Vojvoda is Repic. It's the accused who continues to make that link. The witness has been quite clear about what his evidence is. So the question should be put in a way which correctly reflects what the witness's evidence is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the witness's words, here they are: "A Chetniks called Vojvoda, his surname Repic, I do not know his first name, together with the Chetnik that was called Zoks took out both the two other Muslims in front of the building and beat them with various heavy items, heavy objects." That's what the witness said, "Vojvoda whose surname was Repic." And that's what it says here and it's quite clear from this document. So I don't know what English translation you have there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Then the question should be put that this is -- this is now being quoted from the 1993 statement. The witness has explained extensively about this, and his evidence today is different. So that's where the confusion come in. When the statement from 1993 which the witness is not standing by today is being cited as his evidence today confusion arise and that's my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, just a minute. You're just saying that the witness does not stand by what he said in 1993. This is not what I understood. You are interpreting it this way. The question remains as follows: Who is this Vojvoda? In 1993, the witness says that he was called Repic. This is what we have. The accused is telling us that this man Repic is in fact Dusan Vuckovic, who was tried and convicted for that. This is what I understood, but maybe I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Maybe we should not get into submissions in front of the witness if we want to clarify this with him later, but I just say that I -- I don't have the same understanding of the witness evidence. Maybe if there's time for redirect I can also try to clean it up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must admit that in this courtroom we've had Prosecutor's who had a much better understanding of things, but before I started I said that I was coming back to this document. This has to be recorded in the transcript, if not, then it has been video recorded. I said we're coming back to the documents. I tried to cut a long story short and confirm what he had already confirmed and we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In other words, a Chetnik whom they called Vojvoda, whose surname was Repic, and whose first name I didn't know, together with another Chetnik called Zoks took out this man," I don't want to mention his name, "and in front of the building they beat him with various hard objects. When they were tired, they put him back into the room." And this corresponds to what really happened, doesn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: "They did the same with another man." Again I don't want to mention his name. "After them it was my turn. When I was taken out, they ordered me to lift my arms above my head and they started beating me with an iron rod in the area of my chest and stomach." Does this correspond to the facts, the truthful facts, and the things that you went through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: "After the beating was over, they put me back in the room. On the way back to the room I learnt that one of the previous men had succumbed to the beating and died." And you know who that is. We don't want to close this session. We don't want to mention any names, but let me ask you whether this is a fact, whether this is the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: "After an hour, we were assigned to go to Zvornik to a new prison, the so-called New Izvor. We set out straight away, and the body of the person who had died remained where he died, in that same room." Does this reflect the fact -- the facts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He remained behind. He stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: "It was only the following day when the reminder of the detainees arrived in Zvornik did I learn from a man called Juso, who had also worked in the same company and whose family name I can't remember, that the body of the deceased and two other men who had also died, i.e., according to Juso, they had been killed from a rifle, were transported to Zvornik." And this man who was with you and who died of the beating, this man from Zvornik, was taken to a village where he was buried. Does this reflect the facts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does not in the way it was worded. I heard that these two men had been shot and that the man who was buried in Zvornik had succumbed to the wounds similar to the first man. It's not the same situation. I didn't say that all of them shot from a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I am clear on that. The person who was with you succumbed to the beating wounds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the other two were shot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the three of them were transported to Zvornik, and then the first person who died from beating was transported to the village from which he hailed and where he was buried.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was first transported to hospital, and then his father took his body from the hospital and took him to the village. I suppose that's how it happened. And then he was buried in the village near Zvornik, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So there's nothing in dispute here then. "On the 16th of May," I believe it says on the 16th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think we will have to look into the translation. I just wanted to place on record that in the English translation of the statement I have I cannot see the reference to any shooting, but if -- I mean I take it the accused has read out correctly what's in the statement, but there's an issue we will have to come back to later, but in the interests of time I'm just placing this on the record so we can sort it out later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I did make a note of the fact that we do not know how these people died. It's you who mentioned the shooting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, occasions I have told you that your translation services are really poor. It says here, and the witness can confirm it, that the body of the person who died of beating and who was with him, and two other detainees who also died, i.e., according to Juso, had been killed with a rifle." This is what the original text reads. How this was translated, God only knows who your translators are and what their intentions are, what hidden agendas they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: "Those bodies were transported to Zvornik, and the person who succumbed to the beating from Zvornik was transported to his village where he was buried." This is what the original reads. Is this how you read it, Mr. VS-1015?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is something to that effect but my sight is really poor and the copy is not clear and there are things I don't understand. The copy is rather blurred. So I was not able to follow all that. I could not read all that. But something to that effect happened. I don't know how this was recorded. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There's no need for you to help the Prosecutor, not even God can help him, so entangled they are in the false indictment, but look at the next passage. It says they were killed from a rifle. Do you see that? Do you see that in the penultimate sentence from that passage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to find the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The first long passage, the penultimate line in that passage. "Killed from a rifle." This is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Maybe somebody who speaks Serbian among the registry staff could help you and show you where it says that they were killed from a rifle. I don't see any other way?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can that be done?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters interpreted as you said, that they were killed by shooting. So go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Prosecution is guilty of this confusion, because they say that it doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It says here that you stated that this person died of old age, and later on you said that he died of a heart attack.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must have forgotten in the meantime. In any case, I didn't say that he was killed with a rifle. I stated that he died of old age or natural causes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: These mistakes are quite possible in anybody's memory, and I am not holding it against you. It does happen that you think that you said one thing and you actually said something else. Even science can justify such memory errors, so I'm not disputing anything here. Let's move on to the next passage. "In the Novi Izvor prison in Karakaj I stayed up to the 15th of July, 1992. Throughout all this time, I was occasionally ill-treated and physically abused. When I was interviewed about different circumstances, I allege -- I allegedly stated that all Serb children should be slaughtered and also spoke about which Serbs smuggled weapons to the Muslims. Since I did not know that, I could not have answered any of those questions either, and that's why I was beaten with various objects." Does this reflect the truth? Does this reflect the facts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know the answers, and that's why I was beaten. I had to spend 10 or 12 days in bed after the beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not disputing that. I just want you to confirm this. I'm convinced that this is really what happened. I'm not disputing that this really happened to you. And terrible things happened to you, there's no doubt about that in my mind. "I was beaten by a Chetnik whom they called Zoks. Pufta took out and beat," a name is mentioned here. I suppose we can mention it in open session because it was mentioned by other witnesses. If the Prosecution does not object. If there is an objection, then I will not mention the name. Can I mention the name of the person without the transcript having to be redacted? This person was a victim, was killed in Zvornik, and there's no doubt about that. Can I say his name?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: "He beat Cirak Ismet who died of the wounds as a result of the beating. Pufta is a Chetnik from the -- Serbia, probably from around Valjevo or maybe Kraljevo. He's a younger man. He's 19, well built. His hair is something between blonde and black, and his characteristic feature is that he screams when he beats people. Zoks is also from Serbia. He is tall, thin. He has curly black hair. And together with him was also Dragan called Toro, and he was their captain." Does all this reflect the facts as you saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment. Give me a moment, please. It's correct about Pufta, correct about Dragan Toro, and to does correspond with Ismet Cirak. And now as to what happened at Ekonomija, that he took people out at Ekonomija, I don't remember that, but I only know that what he did, he did to Ismet Cirak. And I'm talking about Pufta. And it is true that he was strong, young, that he had a big head, short hair, that he was rather aggressive. Sometimes he would come in a tracksuit. Sometimes he would be wearing a uniform when he came.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's move on then. "The aforementioned Pufta took it out on some individuals. On the right arm of a detainee Muslim he carved out a piece of skin with a tattoo of a moon and star." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: "On the 15th of July, 1992, 29 of us from Izvor Karakaj were transported to the Batkovic camp together with three other busloads from the so-called Novi Izvor prison in Zvornik. When we arrived in Batkovic, we were also exposed to various ill-treatment and beatings on the part of the guards there and all those who were either there or who would come to the camp. Among them, the worst was a person called Velo. He was the guard's commander, also the guard Glogor, the guard called Major and Zoran Zaric, and the others whose names I cannot remember." Does all this reflect the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but let me just correct you. It's not Glogor but Gligor. The name is Gligor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes it must be a typo but here it says Glogor. "In addition to the physical and psychological abuse in the camp, we did not have any hygiene facilities. The circumstances of life were bad. The conditions were bad. We were billeted in the tents when the temperature outside was 35 degrees, and in the tent the temperature must have been around 50 degrees Centigrade, and we were not allowed to leave the tent. "On the 17th of August, 1992, a delegation of the International Red Cross came to Batkovici and then we were registered as detainees. From then on the situation improved a little, and the situation remained as so until the moment when I was exchanged on the 21st of June, 1993. "I have nothing further to add to this except for the fact that my -- this statement contains all of my words. That's why I recognise the statement as my own, and I sign it, and I would like to add that I am prepared to testify about all this before any court." Does this reflect the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does reflect the truth, but if something else appeared in the following statements it must have just been an extension of the topics and hence a possible discrepancy, but whatever is in the statement is true, and I don't see how it could have been any worse than it really was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-1015, terrible things happened to you. There's no doubt about that. They could not have been worse. The only worse thing would have been if you died.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only say that in Ciglana I fell and almost succumbed and to the illness on 10 or 15 occasions, but let me confirm that people from Novi Sad whose nicknames was -- nickname was Lala, I would fall down on the concrete from fear and every time I thought I would die. But then I would come to. To my biggest surprise it was all terrible. It was horrendous. I'm sure that there are even wore things, but I'm really still at a loss to understand how people can do such things to other people. I consider myself a human being and I would like to remain so until the day I die.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you believe me when I tell you that I sympathise and empathise with your sufferings, or maybe you think I'm just acting before the Trial Chamber and the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose I can believe you. You've stated it publicly before this Trial Chamber, so I suppose it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I can even tell you that I don't even care what the Trial Chamber or the Prosecution are going to think about me and what the sentence is going to be. I'm just afraid of God and nobody else. Do you believe me when I tell you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe you if you put it that way. I suppose that you are telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But, Mr. VS-1015, where in your statement are Seselj's men? You don't mention my name at all. You don't mention any Seseljevci men. You are not talking about Seselj's corps from Novi Sad. There are no Seselj's sabotage units. There is none of that. How come it's not there, Mr. VS-1015?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how this came about. You yourself said how many years have elapsed. The date may be there. I don't know. How this was, how fast this was all said and done, I don't know. Later on I recalled things. Things came back to mind. They surfaced in my memory. I haven't made anything up. I simply extended my statement. I told you about this Repic, this Pony-tail. Perhaps I heard that that was his nickname when I got out. If we were to go on talking about details like this, I might recall something or forget something. So please understand. After all these years, after five years, you can't say things in exactly the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I understand that completely, but, Mr. VS-1015, the memory grows weaker in time. It cannot be added to in time except through imagination or suggestions coming from the outside. You gave a statement on the 22nd of December, 1993, and you were exchanged on the 21st of July, 1993. So the statement was given five months after your exchange, and that was when your memory was freshest. I assume that in those first few months you relived everything in your dreams at night. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You dreamed the people -- of the people who had been killed, had been tortured along with you. Along with you, you must have dreamed about your torturers also. Did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. What do you expect? Mr. Seselj, when the war was still going on, shells were still landing where I was. Would you expect me to sing songs or to think or dream about anything else in that war? It wasn't that I got out and then I could dream this or that. The war was still going on. Everything was still dark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we understand all that very well, but we're trying to shed some light on this aspect. Here you're speaking about the Chetniks. Today during your testimony you spoke about the Seselj's men. Do try and remember. Could it be that you heard about this after the events that you heard about the fact that the Chetniks were Seselj's men? Could it be that you heard it then, or are you sure that during -- that you heard that during the events, that you heard it from those men that they were Seselj's men? That's my first thing. Second thing I'd like to elicit from you: At some point in time you said that it was Niski who told you that he was one of Seselj's men. So I didn't quite understand whether you heard it from Niski alone or whether you heard it also from the other men who abused you, who tortured you, because whilst you said that Niski did nothing, that you did not see him torture people. So try to really focus on this, because your testimony today is the most important thing for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why I didn't mention here, it's possible that in that environment I didn't mention it after that, but I say again that Niski said that when he described that incident the last time, and in Ciglana there were two of those men who I mentioned before working as mechanics, and I heard that from Niski himself. And later on through the stories of the employees there with whom we socialised and spent time, they said that they were members of Seselj's sabotage unit. That's what the man himself said. I would like to meet up with this Captain Niski. I don't know whether he's from Nis or not and whether he's a captain or not, but I would like to meet him. Why I didn't say that then? Well, it was a long time ago and I may have spoken in haste. You can see that the statement was only two pages long. I was not making the statement before a court. I just signed what they put down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, here's my problem: The War Crimes Commission then sitting in Tuzla, that is five months after your release, met with you. Well, I was not a member of committee, but I suppose what the committee members wanted to know, who had committed those crimes. Who were the people responsible for them. Therefore, you gave a statement. We all have this statement here, and in at no time, in no place is there any mention of Seselj's men. You do indeed speak of the Chetniks, but we find nowhere any mention of Seselj's men. How is it that several years later you suddenly remember things, and there is Zoks, there's Toro, and all these people somehow magically become Seselj's men. What is your explanation for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I made this statement, which I'm now seeing for the first time, and where things are written as they were, but I can hardly remember where -- when this was. However, the statement I made to The Hague investigators, this went on for three or four days. And when we talked then these topics cropped up, and each incident was dealt with in detail. So I knew all these things even though I hadn't said them before. I state again that Niski said they were Seselj's sabotage unit, and I say it again. If I failed to mention it that time I don't know why, but later on I did say that they belonged to that unit and that they themselves said that before witnesses. They said it in front of other people. Other people also know this. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This morning, page 59, line 19, you said: "Seselj, I don't know you." Well, back then when these events that occurred, events you were a victim of, this isn't challenged by no one, had you already heard the name of Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have said I don't know him personally. I did hear about him, and he appeared on television when there were elections in the former Yugoslavia when parties were established. I think Mr. Seselj would agree he was the leader of a political party. I don't remember its name. I think it was the Radicals or something like that, I'm not sure. And I knew him in that way, but I didn't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, when Niski told you that this was Seselj's men or Seselj's sabotage unit, you thought that was logical and true to form?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Because when he mentioned that, I immediately concluded that that's how it was, because he said it. I'm not saying that Seselj fired shots or killed people. I don't know anything about that. But Seselj's name was mentioned, and they said they were in his sabotage unit. He mentioned a sabotage unit. I repeat. And if Niski and Dragan Toro and some others hadn't been there, they would turn up for a day or two and then people would continue working probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-1015, for years there were anecdotes bandied about in public about Seselj's submarines which can travel down the River Sava as far as Zagreb. People spoke of Seselj's rockets, of Seselj's air force, but this is the first time I've heard of Seselj's sabotage units. Nobody ever heard of any such thing until it turned up in your statement. Absolutely nobody ever heard of any sabotage units of Seselj's. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I may have mentioned units in my statement, but it was more like a sabotage group. I may have mentioned this before. I may have said units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's misleading the witness. The same thing was said yesterday, for example.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not misleading at all. I'm on the right track here, and I'm showing that using the tragedy of this witness and his sufferings, he has been manipulated. His sufferings and his tragedy have been manipulated quite evidently and misused.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can we again see on the internal screen which the public can't see a Prosecution document shown to us the day before yesterday. It's 02208. It's been admitted into evidence, but I don't know under what number because I still haven't received the exhibit register. It's 65 ter 02208, and it was shown in the courtroom the day before yesterday. Can we see it on our internal screens and not have the name of the person under the drawing identified. I think you can do that. Not even this witness needs to know the name of the other witness. Can you zoom in a little bit where we see this building. Zoom in a little bit where the building is and the floors are marked. You see, a witness who testified here before you spoke about the building you were in. You may have been there together, but I won't mention his name. And he said that this administrative building --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This witness was not at that location. This is a sketch of the Standard factory, and this witness was not at Standard.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it's possible they were together in the Ciglana, and this is the Standard administrative building, which I'm showing for quite another reason, not to prove that the witness was in that building but to show that another witness here marked who was where in that building on each floor, and the ground floor, which is marked here, it says "Reconnaissance men and sabotage men." On the second floor Loznicani, the people from Loznica, and the military police. On the second floor prisoners and Seselj's men. So you see, this witness drew distinction between the sabotage men and Seselj's men, and you are referring to Seselj's sabotage men. The problem was caused by someone who suggested to both witnesses that they should mention Seselj's men and sabotage men. So one person mentioned them separately, Seselj's men and sabotage men, and you compounded the two together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What do you say to this, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't want to comment on this drawing, on this sketch. I don't know anything about this building. I know about the Standard building, where it is, but I've never been inside so I can't recognise this. And what he wrote down, well, that's his business. I don't want to go into that. But I have to tell you again. I may have misspoken when I said units, but this person did say Seselj's sabotage men. I am sure that that's what he said. I assert that before all these people. They were called Seselj's men. They were from Kraljevo. They said that they would send the loot back to Kraljevo and things like that so that they were constantly referred to as Seselj's men, men from Kraljevo, men from Loznica, and so on. This is something quite different. This is a quite different location which I've never seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, just a minute. I have my eyes on the stopwatch. You normally have 25 minutes left. If the Prosecutor has no redirect, we may continue to 1.30, have another -- an extra 15 minutes and stop. It all depends on Mr. Marcussen. Do you have any redirect or not? If so, I believe we will have to resume next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm willing not to put any questions. Of course I have -- it's difficult for me to say what will arise during the next 25 minutes, but at this stage I don't have any questions that I need to put in redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, please try and finish up and you will have used up your two hours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will certainly complete my examination. I have never overstepped my time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I believe you when you say that one man mentioned sabotage men, Seselj's sabotage men, and so on. I believe that, Mr. VS-1015, but this did not happen when you were incarcerated. It happened a few years after that, and that is where we differ.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. That was said in the Ciglana at the gate when Mr. Niski, and I have to reiterate I'm speaking the truth, I never saw him mistreating anyone, and sometimes he even saved people to prevent that monster, I won't even call him a Chetnik, that monster who was mistreating those people from doing it. And there was a man from my village who was a guard there and who protected me, who stopped me from going out at that point. And when Niski arrived and his car brakes screeched, he must have been passing down excuse me, I'm talking very fast I'll try to calm down. When he saw what was going on, the car stopped, he cocked his pistol with his left hand and pointed at that man and those guards, and he saved those people from mistreatment, and he ordered them to be washed because they were all covered in blood. And then he told that man about those sabotage men and that's when it started to be mentioned. So is it clear to you now Mr. Seselj? I really don't know what else to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, everything is clear to me and I understand your situation also. Was your name familiar to you many years before the war? Did you hear of me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. Not long before the war, but when the political parties were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear that I was sentenced to eight years in prison as an anti-Communist, a nationalist, and so on in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't hear it at the time. I may have heard it after the war, six or seven years after the war, but these political things, well, I wasn't really -- I'll not really following the current affairs in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I want to know what you heard of me. Do you know that I held a rally in Mali Zvornik before the war and that there was an incident at that rally, that some people from Veliki Zvornik came and that they threw stones at us and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know that. I don't know. I was not in Mali Zvornik. I lived a bit further away from Zvornik. This must have happened while I did not need to go there because I lived on the other side from Zvornik so this must have been happened unbeknownst to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you must have heard of Seselj's volunteers during the war in the former Croatian federal unit. I'm sure that you have heard of the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party. I'm sure that you heard of them before the war started in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was this war in Croatia and this was aired on TV. Whatever I could hear I could hear it on TV, on Belgrade 1 or 2. I had only these two channels that were available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And in 1991 you must have heard on St. George's day that I went to Sarajevo and I was supposed to appear and on a Sarajevo TV show that was hosted by a Aleksandar Tijanic and Mirjana Bobic-Mojsilovic, it had a large viewing on Yutel. And then there were demonstrations before the national theatre against my appearance on TV and there were incidents during those demonstrations. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am familiar with Tijanic. The name rings a bell, but again I don't remember that case. I was a good man. I was an honest man. I was a good worker. I had a firm. My family was really good and I spent much more time doing other stuff than -- than following politics. I was never interested in political speeches or shows of political nature. They all were -- went past me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There were some shortages before the war. There were shortages of oil, flour, sugar. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember anecdotes where people would write on the windows of shops, sugar is coming, and then some other people would be replacing it with Seselj's coming?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my village there were only two or three small shops, and those people who worked in the shops were Serbs and this is not very likely that somebody would write something like that on a shop with -- in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In any case you knew quite a lot about me. You were familiar with my name and all of these things and in Zvornik what happened and the things that you testify about. I'm sure that you could not have overheard the name of Seselj's volunteers being mentioned as torturers or sabotage men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now you said it yourself that Seselj's sabotage men weren't mentioned. They were mentioned. They were in -- under your control, maybe not, but their name did come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. It must have been striking and I'm sure that you could not have ignored that when you provided your statement in 1993 to the Muslim authorities. My name was so well-known amongst Muslims and across the territory of the former Yugoslavia that you could not overheard my name being mentioned. If anybody mentioned my name during your torture, during your ordeal, I'm sure that you would have told that to the Muslim authorities. I'm sure they must have even asked you about Seselj and Seselj's volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody asked me anything. I was only there for a brief time. After the war I crossed -- went across Croatia and further on. Let me not tell you where I went, I went on foot. I was never in favour of war. I never participated in any war, and I really wondered all the time and I still keep on wondering how come that I was not guilty of everything, that I was blameless, I still had to go through all that ordeal. And it is always like that, only the weak and innocent suffer in -- in wars.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I agree with you, but Mr. VS-1015 today for the first time you mentioned that this Caca person from the Novi Sad Corps was also a Seselj's volunteer. You never mentioned it to anybody before, either to The Hague Tribunal in any of the other statements. You've mentioned this for the first time today. How come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe this was not recorded. I must have said it. Maybe it wasn't recorded. I was not alone there. If there are any other witnesses of these events I'm sure that they will tell you that this Caca existed. That was his nickname. Let me describe you: He was about 50 years of age; he has always had his sleeves rolled up; he wore a military blouse and old military trousers of the JNA, olive drab trousers, and this person didn't do any harm to me. He saved a few of us who were there in sand, lying in the sand when Mr. Zoks cocked a pistol that he was carrying as a souvenir. It was a long-barrelled pistol, Colt. He fired shots above our heads and he had ordered us to lie down. I was towards the end of that row of detainees and I was covered with the pebbles. I thought I was dead. I could not believe myself that I was alive, and this person Caca came closer to Zoks and told him, "What are you doing? Leave people alone, they are working." So whatever you want from me, Mr. Seselj, if you get to this Caca, to this Zoks, and the other people who were there, ask them whether that is correct or not. I'm sure that you will be able to obtain information. I'm sure that you're willing to get information. I'm talking about the -- not only about the worst things but also about things that -- and people who saved us at one point or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not contesting the existence of that person Caca, but I'm contesting the existence of the Novi Sad Corps of socials volunteers. Where does this come from? You had stated that earlier today you said that Caca belonged to the Novi Sad Corps of Seselj's volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were telling us that themselves. They didn't stay there long. They were all constantly on the move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please speak slower. You're going too fast. We need a break between questions and answers. And please try to be more concise in your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the Yellow Wasps in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard it here -- or before another court actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that the commander of the Yellow Wasps was Vojin Vuckovic also known as Zuco?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possible, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yesterday before this Trial Chamber and the Prosecution I provided the statement of this Vojin Vuckovic person that was given to my associates in order to be used in this trial. In this statement he says, and I'm not going to read his entire statement, I'm just going paraphrase it. He says in this statement that the Kraljevo group of volunteers consisted of 52 members belonged to the White Eagles, i.e., to the Serb popular renovation movement. This is not what I said. But Zuco was there and he knows who the others who were there were and he says that the Kraljevo group belonged to the White Eagles. Do you think that this is possible or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know what the person told you. Again I repeat Niski told us that. Look for Niski and ask him. That's what he said. And of course that the story was all about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But he says about Niski that he belonged to the Arkan's men. He says that the person called Dragan, family name unknown, nickname Niski belonged to the Serbian volunteers guard. This is what Zuco says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do I know? We were ill-treated. That's all I know. Niski didn't say I am this and that. Dragan did not introduce himself to us and said who he belonged to. That was the whole atmosphere. That's how things went. Later on when they processed us, when we were working they even removed some of their insignia. If there were -- had not been other people who beat us in Ciglana, we had even become friends with those people from Seselj's group. We worked with them and there were no other incidents but the two involving Zoks who shot at us and Pufta who did what he did with these two people, and from then on when Pufta did what he did, then they removed both Zoks and Pufta and during the following days until the moment we were transported to Batkovic they never appeared again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In his statement Zuco says that the group under Pivarski's command had a total of 16 volunteers and that they did not belong to the Serbian Radical Party. And Zuco knows. He was there. And there is no reason for him to lie because I attacked him a number of times publicly, so there is no reason for him to speak in my favour because I attacked him so many times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not testifying against Zuco. I'm just telling you how it was. If you can bring Zuco as your own witness or whatever his name is, if you can bring him over as your own witness, then he can repeat what you're claiming here as a witness before this Trial Chamber, and I -- there's nothing for me to object about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In his statement he says that Sasa, whom you also mentioned -- you mentioned Sasa, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That this Sasa led a group of some 15 to 20 volunteers from Mali Zvornik and that they also did not belong to the Serbian Radical Party volunteers. That's what Zuco says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he says what he says. Now you can actually understand how many people beat us there, how many people went through there, and it is only a miracle that we all survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I really can't know how many people beat you. I can either believe you or not. And what you said in your first statement in 1993, I believe you, but I'm saying that it was not the Seselj's group that beat you. We have another statement that deals with Pivarski. It is only one passage long. Can this please be put on the ELMO. We did not see it yesterday. This is a statement provided by Savo Sinadinovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listen, we have to finish within a few minutes, especially because we're just sort of repeating the same things over and over. No need to show the statement. Put your question. Say that there is a statement saying this and that, and ask the witness for an answer. You've been trying to elicit from the witness something that he doesn't want to say. You've been doing this for two hours. Now ask a question without speaking about this statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I achieved everything I wanted from this witness. If you are not willing to notice that and if that is not your conclusion that's up to you. I'm not interested in that. I have proven that this witness's suffering, this witness's ordeal, had been instrumentalised and that his current statement does not reflect the facts. The only statement that is truthful is his first statement and everything else was just a build-up from elsewhere. I have nothing personal against this witness. I have led my counter-evidence. I've proved what I wanted to prove able sure that the general public will understand that this witness has been instrumentalised for some political goals without any blame of his own. I'm not going ask him any more questions. I finished my cross-examination. Thank you very much, sir, that you have helped me do what I wanted to do even against your will.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I thank you on behalf of the Trial Chamber for your testimony. Of course you have all our sympathy and compassion for all your sufferings. We have a few seconds left before we adjourn, and I want to tell the parties, the Prosecution and Mr. Seselj, that apparently the witness scheduled next week will not be testifying. Therefore, yesterday we asked for VS-33 could come. There still has been no answer so far. We asked the Prosecution to start the hearing with the viewing of video clips. Mr. Marcussen, do you have a specific stance or not? What about next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The Prosecution is looking into these options. I don't think we have reached any conclusion. I cannot add anything to what Mr. Mundis said yesterday, but it might be possible that tomorrow we can inform Your Honours about what we will be in a position to present during next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. At any rate, the next hearing will take place on Tuesday at 2.15 in the afternoon as scheduled. Thank you. We shall reconvene on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 1st day of April, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.26 p.m.,
